reviews.text: Good place to stop for a quick dinner or getting together with friends. Very casual atmosphere. Not too dark nor too bright lighting. Some dishes may be a bit salty. My smashburger comes with the sauce. A bit salty for my taste. The place also serve Mexican dishes as well...may be next time. So 🌝

This was my second time here and both times I ordered the buffalo chicken sandwich, which was really delicious. As well as the Cajun fries which were equally as tasty! On my second visit I ordered the Peanut Chocolate Vanilla milkshake. For a price of $200 I had high hopes that it would be on par with or better than other “American” restaurants in the area, but was really disappointed. It was incredibly sweet, chocolate sauce covering the glass and on the whipped cream, and it seems the blender isn’t of best quality because there were still chunks of ice. It was so sweet that I could barely drink it. I got it to go, but had no desire to even finish it…I’ll come back though! Everything else is great, but I definitely won’t try the milkshakes again.

Absolutely amazing burger place. We were so hungry and saw this driving past so we thought let’s give it a try. Numerous options for burgers as well as Mexican cuisine. Everything was of generous portion and was super tasty. Finally found a place with great Caesar salad dressing. Burgers we super yummy and juicy.

I ordered Uber eats from Beast Bar&Grill. I had the Sloppy Moe. It was fairly flavoured, not something I would order again. I think if it was hot it would have been much better. But even with it being hot I am not sure the flavour would have been there why I am giving it a 5.8 The crinkle cut fries was what was expected of them and nothing special 6.5. Over all I would not recommend ordering Uber Eats from this shop.
I have issues with the adding of 10% service or whatever charge onto a bill.  Just price the items fully in the first instance.  Any other practice feels slightly scammy.

reviews.text:
SHO is Kaohsiung’s first Michelin-starred restaurant, proudly holding a one-star rating. Both the dining environment and the dishes truly live up to Michelin standards. Reservations can be made through Inline, and there is no dress code. If you have any dietary restrictions, you can communicate with the restaurant in advance. For example, one of our elders doesn’t eat beef, so the restaurant kindly substituted it with Taiwan’s premium choho Pork(究好豬).

The cuisine combines elements of Japanese kaiseki and French fine dining, but most of the ingredients are locally sourced, featuring seasonal seafood and vegetables from Taiwan. The full course consists of eight dishes, with options to pair with either wine or tea.

I highly recommend the kamameshi! Today, we had two different variations: Hokkaido salmon roe and Australian beef/Taiwanese pork. The beef version was particularly impressive, seasoned with Sichuan pepper, adding a unique and delicious twist. Pairing it with the restaurant’s yuzu-pickled daikon gave it a refreshing contrast, making for an interesting flavor experience!

The sashimi was aged, resulting in a delicate texture that melted in my mouth—I really enjoyed it. As for the other dishes, I found them to be safe and somewhat unremarkable. The most highly praised dish online, the salad, was just okay for me. It featured a variety of vegetables prepared in different ways—raw, fried, and pickled—creating a complex mix of flavors and textures. However, it almost felt too complex, making the overall taste a bit confusing.

For dessert, I preferred the monaka(最中) over the strawberry lavender mousse. However, I personally felt that neither dessert matched well with the courses. I would have enjoyed a tea-based dessert pairing instead.

We had a wonderful dinner experience. The staff were exceptionally accommodating, and the food was outstanding. Everything was perfectly executed, and we even enjoyed a nice chat with the chef about our favorite dishes.

I have never written a two star review nor do I ever wish to write another one.  My only reasons for it are quite simple, you should address the issues at the restaurant, and see what could be done there and then. Taking the anger home and antagonizing the restaurant is unfair and should not be done lightly.

We were excited to celebrate my mom’s birthday with her first omakase at Sho, a sister restaurant of Den in Kaohsiung. To my surprise, we were first seated in the inside room, then at a table, with no prior warning about the possibility of not seating at the dining counter, which was a key part of the experience. By the time we settled in, everyone else was already seated. The reservation only mentioned that seats couldn’t be requested, but didn’t indicate there were alternative options to the counter seating. All we asked for was prior communication; the lack of it left a sour taste before we even started.
Both my wife and mom had stomach cramps, so we requested hot tea with the meal. Sho said the chef could not serve hot tea because it would detract from its nuances, offering only hot water or cold-brewed tea instead. It felt odd for a Japanese restaurant.
Overall, the meal was tasty, the salad was nicely done and invokes alot of Michel Bra ethos.  But my mom encountered a large sinew in her sashimi tuna that was impossible to chew. We voiced this issue, yet received no acknowledgment throughout dinner. Regarding the taste of the dishes, it seemed like kuzu and sansho were used quite liberally.  Two dishes had sauces thickened with kuzu, and Sansho leaves appeared in the shime course, and also in the sauce for the grilled chicken previously, nothing wrong with it.  But i’ve been taught to not repeat ingredients during the experience of a tasting menu.

The final course was a chocolate mousse monaka served with hot oolong tea. Since we had requested hot tea earlier, it felt like we were being toyed with. Three different staff members later provided conflicting reasons for why hot tea wasn’t served initially.

1. Hot tea does not match with the courses served, therefore we will not serve it.  - Surely a hot tea is a better match than me drinking a ice cold suntory beer to go with the strawberry lavender mousse served with micro oregano and macerated strawberries.

2. The chef does not believe he can make a good enough hot tea to be served during dinner service - then why didn’t you just serve me the same oolong tea in the beginning of the meal?

3. The chef does feel that the nuances of the tea varieties can be properly displayed with hot service - then why didn't you just serve me the hot oolong in the beginning?

Chef Fujimoto-san believed the tuna was fine to serve, claiming the sinew was actually delicious. If that’s the case, why didn’t all three of us receive it?  The sous chef Jason seemed upset that I didn’t grasp their service approach, but they overlooked the fundamental rule of hospitality—making guests happy. All I wanted was hot tea for my wife and mom’s cramps. First denied, then served as part of the meal, it felt like they wanted to make a fool out of us.

In full disclosure, they removed the service charge from my bill, but it didn’t ease the unease or the disappointment on my mom's 60th birthday. While this may seem ridiculous centered on a cup of tea, it highlights a broader issue of hospitality that was completely neglected.

Tucked away in a quiet corner, 承 Sho offers a dining experience that is both intimate and exceptional. From the moment you step inside, the minimalist yet warm decor sets the tone for what promises to be a thoughtfully curated culinary journey. The ambiance is serene, with soft lighting and elegant, understated furnishings that create a perfect backdrop for the star of the show—the food.

The menu at 承 Sho is a masterful blend of traditional Japanese techniques and contemporary flavors. Each dish is meticulously prepared, showcasing the chef's deep respect for ingredients and attention to detail. The nigiri is impressive, with rice that is perfectly seasoned and at the ideal temperature, allowing the quality of the fish to shine.

The service is attentive without being intrusive, and the staff is knowledgeable about both the food and the extensive sake selection. They are more than willing to guide you through the menu, offering suggestions that enhance the overall experience.

One of the highlights of the meal was the omakase option, where the chef takes you on a journey through the best seasonal offerings. Each course is a surprise, and every bite feels like a revelation, with flavors that are perfectly balanced and presentation that is both artful and restrained.

承 Sho is not just a meal; it's an experience. It's a place where the simplicity of the dishes belies the complexity of the flavors, and where every detail is considered to create a harmonious dining experience. Whether you're a seasoned aficionado of Japanese cuisine or a curious newcomer, 承 Sho is a place that will leave a lasting impression. Highly recommended for anyone looking to indulge in a sophisticated and authentic Japanese dining experience.

Let's start with the food: meticulously plated with grace, using premium ingredients from both Japan and local Taiwan. Although it was star worthy, something was missing; seemed an appropriate and traditional kaiseki ryōri yet fusioned with Kaohsiung style. Taste was definitely amongst the top but nothing I particular stood out for the wow factor.

Atmosphere: Michelin worthy, staff was professional, well mannered and paid attention to all details of the guests. Everything was placed with thought and consideration to the customer. Environment was nice and spacious, allowing customers to fully see two huge food preparation islands and the back end; shows craftsmanship of how a proper kitchen is ran. Dishes were explained in details and of course catering to food choices.

Menu change every 3 months!

You can order the paella with noodles instead. The rice was cooked with squid ink which stained my mouth. A drink of water washes the ink down. There is a distinct taste to the squid ink. We visited Kaoshiong for the first time and this was our first meal/dinner. We were very impressed by the cute homey interior and welcomed with nice service.

The homemade food style tasted good and we chose how spicy we'd like the dishes to be. We liked the fried chicken dish and the fish. The pork stew wasn't very tender and had a dry texture. The radish soup was a bit fishy to our taste.

Overall we had a great experience there and had a taste of Taiwanese home cooked food.

Very rare authentic Taiwanese home cooking inside a uniquely decorated Taiwanese home.  Fun experience!! Must try!!

Fixed menu. Very good price $350/person for two with 5 dishes and 1 soup.

The owner is a young family where the husband is a self taught chef.  They’re both super friendly, and welcome you in like you’re entering their home. Chef is incredibly humorous, even comes out to chat with you, and share his story with you.

Very impressive grannie’s style of Taiwanese cuisine. You can tell the chef really spend lots of efforts on what he serves. The whole experience of having dinner here is really comfortable and cozy, just like pop into a friend’s flat. Will absolutely visit here more.

Do book a table before your visiting!!!
A must visit in Kaohsiung. If you don't mind a surprise set menu based on the fresh ingredients of the day, this is for you.

This Hong-Kong-style restaurant's menu includes a selection of dim sum (both traditional versions and more modern takes) and Cantonese barbecued meats. We were seated in one of their private rooms for a large party, and the service was attentive and personal.

The highlight of the meal was our pre-ordered roasted goose. That's right, not the typical duck on the menu, but goose. It was prepared and served as 4 separate courses, each with a different cooking method: crispy skin wraps, sliced breast/leg, stir-fried bones, and bone porridge/congee. Every preparation was excellent, and the goose meat was flavorful and tender.

The dim sum and other dishes were good, with another standout being the tofu pudding dessert at the end.

We had roasted duck with 4 different dishes. Good quality of food and great service. Nice decor as well. Each table has privacy without listening other table’s conversation. This is probably the best Cantonese Dim Sum place in HK.

The taro tapioca soup was pretty good,  not overly sweet.
Delicious food and good services.

reviews.text:
Delicious 肉燥飯 or 滷肉飯 here. Half cooked fried egg very delicious to pair with the rice. Bamboo shoots soup is a must try! Just subtly sweet, pairs very well with the rice braised pork rice.
Strict protocol for dinning in or takeaway. Order & pay before taking seats.

Overall waited about 40 minutes to include ordering and waiting for food. They need to fix their ordering system. If people are just ordering the rice and meat, it shouldn't take long at all. Rice is cooked already and meat is cooked already. People ordering other stuff put their order to the side and work on the easier order.

Definitely recommend ordering more than 1 set so it's worth while. Might come again when they first open and to eat inside.
Good local spot serving local Taiwanese favorites... Ordered Lu Rou Fan, Seasoned Duck Egg, Spinach, Tofu, Milk fish Soup... 😋
Nice and fatty braised pork rice. Not overwhelming greasy but with great mouthfeel. Fishball soup was nice and light. Venue is air conditioned and pleasant for a small shop.

Best braised pork rice i ever had in my life. I still can remember the first time i ate this during my trip to Taiwan. The price is also very affordable and the owner of the shop is also very friendly. Damn, i miss this place so much🥲
